objectives.label: Measure arcs from central angles
objectives.description: Determine the measure of an arc as the measure of its central angle, and find the measures of adjacent arcs, semicircles and the circle by adding or subtracting.

objectives.label: Calculate arc length
objectives.description: Calculate the length of an arc as the fraction (measure of the arc / measure of the circle) of the circumference, and compare arcs of equal measure in different circles.

objectives.label: Relate arcs, chords and parallels
objectives.description: Use the corollaries on equal arcs, equal chords and parallel chords or tangents to prove arcs or chords are equal and to find unknown lengths.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; rays MA (upper right) and MB (lower right) from M form angle AMB, meeting the circle at A and B; point C marked on the circle on the left (lower left) on the major arc.

A.why: Shows central angle AMB and its minor and major arcs.

B.why: Shows central angle AMB with minor and major arcs.

entries.text: A central angle is the angle whose vertex is the center of the circle and whose two sides are radii in the circle.

A.why: Central angle is the basis for defining arc measure.

B.why: Defines the central angle on which arc measure rests.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; rays MB (lower left) and MA (lower right) form angle AMB with arrowheads at B and A; point C marked on the circle at top.

A.why: Illustrates central angle and its opposite arcs.

B.why: Shows central angle AMB and its arc.

entries.text: Arc AB is opposite to the central angle AMB, and arc ACB is opposite to the central reflective angle AMB.

A.why: States which arc is opposite which central angle.

B.why: Relates minor and major arcs to central and reflex angles.

entries.text: If angle AMB is a straight angle (AB is a diameter in circle M), then arc AB is congruent to arc ACB and each is called a semicircle.

A.why: Semicircle arises from a straight central angle.

B.why: Semicircle arises when the central angle is straight.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; horizontal diameter BA; radius MC perpendicular to AB (right-angle mark at M) going up to C; radius MD between C and A with angle 60° marked between MA and MD.

A.why: Figure for arc measures equal to central angles.

B.why: Figure showing central angles 90° and 60° whose arc measures are found.

entries.text: The measure of arc AD equals m(∠AMD) = 60°. $m(\overset{\frown}{AD}) = m(\angle AMD) = 60^\circ$

A.why: Arc AD measure equals its central angle.

B.why: Arc measure equals its central angle, 60°.

entries.text: The measure of arc CB equals m(∠CMB) = 90°. $m(\overset{\frown}{CB}) = m(\angle CMB) = 90^\circ$

A.why: Arc CB measure equals its central angle.

B.why: Arc measure equals its central angle, 90°.

entries.text: The measure of arc DC equals m(∠DMC) = 30°. (Why?) $m(\overset{\frown}{DC}) = m(\angle DMC) = 30^\circ$

A.why: Arc DC measure equals its central angle.

B.why: Arc measure equals its central angle, 30°.

entries.text: The measure of arc AB equals m(∠AMB) = 180°. $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\angle AMB) = 180^\circ$

A.why: Arc AB measure equals 180° central angle.

B.why: Arc AB equals its straight central angle, 180°.

entries.text: The measure of the semicircle is 180° and the measure of a circle is 360°. $180^\circ, 360^\circ$

A.why: Semicircle 180° and circle 360°.

B.why: Semicircle is 180° and circle is 360°.

entries.text: Adjacent arcs are two arcs in the same circle that have only one point in common.

A.why: Adjacent arcs are used for adding arc measures.

B.why: Defines adjacent arcs, whose measures are added.

entries.text: Blue circle with centre M (red dot); points A (bottom), B (lower right), C (right) marked by small ticks on the circle.

A.why: Shows adjacent arcs AB and BC.

B.why: Circle with points A, B, C illustrating adjacent arcs.

entries.text: For adjacent arcs AB and BC: m(AB) + m(BC) = m(ABC), so m(AB) = m(ABC) − m(BC). $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) + m(\overset{\frown}{BC}) = m(\overset{\frown}{ABC})$, $m(\overset{\frown}{AB}) = m(\overset{\frown}{ABC}) - m(\overset{\frown}{BC})$

A.why: Add or subtract adjacent arc measures.

B.why: Adding or subtracting adjacent arc measures.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; horizontal diameter BA; radius MC in upper half with 60° between MA and MC; radius MD in lower right with 40° between MA and MD.

A.why: Exercise figure for finding arc measures from angles.

B.why: Central angles of 60° and 40° give arc measures.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, horizontal diameter AB (B left, A right). Radii MC and MD drawn above, D upper left, C upper right; angle CMD marked 70°.

A.why: Exercise figure for finding arc measures by adding or subtracting.

B.why: Diameter and 70° angle used to find arc measures.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, diameter AB (A upper right, B lower left). Radii MD (upper left) and MC (right). Angle AMC = 2x°, angle DMA = 4x°, angle DMB = (3x + 5)°. Values read from figure; verify.

A.why: Exercise figure finding arc measures from angles on a diameter.

B.why: Central angles in algebraic form give arc measures, an exercise on arc measure.

entries.text: Arc length is a part of a circle's circumference proportional with its measure.

A.why: Defines arc length as part of circumference.

B.why: Defines arc length as a part of the circumference.

entries.text: Arc length = (measure of the arc / measure of the circle) × circumference of the circle. $\text{arc length}=\dfrac{\text{measure of the arc}}{\text{measure of the circle}}\times \text{circumference of the circle}$

A.why: Arc length formula from measure fraction.

B.why: Arc length formula as a fraction of the circumference.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, radii MB (left) and MA (lower right); central angle marked 108°.

A.why: Figure of worked example computing arc length.

B.why: Circle with 108° angle for the arc length worked example.

entries.text: Two concentric circles with centre M. Inner (minor) circle radius 7 cm, outer (major) circle radius 14 cm. Points A, B, C, D on the minor circle; E, F, x, y on the major circle. Radii MB-F and MC-x; angle AMB marked 50° and angle CMD marked 50°. Arc AB (minor) and arc CD, arc EF and arc XY (major) are the arcs referred to.

A.why: Concentric circles comparing arcs of equal measure.

B.why: Concentric circles with equal 50° arcs compare arc lengths in different circles.

entries.text: Corollary (1): In the same circle (or in congruent circles), if the measures of arcs are equal, then the lengths of the arcs are equal, and conversely.

A.why: Equal arc measures give equal lengths in same circle.

B.why: Corollary (1) compares lengths of arcs of equal measure.

entries.text: Circle M with points C, D, A, B on the circle; radii MC, MD, MA, MB; angles CMD and AMB each marked with × to show equal measures. Labelled 'In circle M'.

A.why: Shows equal angles giving arcs of equal measure.

B.why: Equal central angles give equal arc lengths, Corollary (1).

entries.text: Circle M with points C, D, A, B on the circle; radii MC, MD, MA, MB; arcs CD and AB marked with // ticks to show equal lengths. Labelled 'And conversely'.

A.why: Shows equal arc lengths conversely.

B.why: Equal arc lengths conversely, illustrating Corollary (1) on arc lengths.

entries.text: Circle M with centre M and points A, B, C, D on it; radii MA, MB, MC, MD drawn, chords AB and CD drawn; angle AMB and angle CMD marked with equal-angle crosses. Labelled 'In circle M'.

A.why: Equal central angles give equal chords.

B.why: Equal central angles give equal chords in the same circle.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and points A, B, C, D; radii MA, MB, MC, MD; chords AB and CD each marked with double tick marks (equal length). Labelled 'And conversely'.

A.why: Equal chords give equal arcs conversely.

B.why: Equal chords imply equal arcs, the converse of the corollary.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and points A, B, C, D on it; radii MD (vertical up), MA, MB, MC drawn; angle AMB marked 60°, angle BMC marked 80°.

A.why: Exercise figure on arcs and chords.

B.why: Central angles 60° and 80° give arc measures to add or subtract.

entries.text: Corollary (3): If two parallel chords are drawn in a circle, then the measures of the two arcs between them are equal.

A.why: Corollary on parallel chords.

B.why: Corollary (3) on parallel chords.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; two parallel horizontal chords AB (upper, through the circle above centre's lower region) and DC (lower), marked parallel with arrows; points B, A on the upper chord, D, C on the lower chord.

A.why: Illustrates parallel chords corollary.

B.why: Two parallel chords illustrate Corollary (3).

entries.text: Corollary (4): If a chord is parallel to a tangent of a circle, then the measures of the two arcs between them are equal.

A.why: Corollary on chord parallel to tangent.

B.why: Corollary (4) on a chord parallel to a tangent.

entries.text: Circle with chord AB (horizontal, marked with an arrow) and a tangent line DC touching the circle at C below it, with arrows at both ends; points B, A on chord, D and C on the tangent line.

A.why: Illustrates chord parallel to tangent.

B.why: Chord parallel to a tangent illustrates Corollary (4).

entries.text: Circle with centre M (dot). Chord EF at top with F at upper left and E at upper right, with an arrow marking it parallel. Chord AB lower, B on left and A on right, with an arrow. Tangent line through C at the bottom of the circle with D marked to the left of C. Lines CF and CE drawn from C to F and E forming a triangle CEF.

A.why: Exercise using parallel chords and tangent.

B.why: Parallel chords and tangent with arcs between them illustrate the parallel corollaries.

entries.text: Circle with centre dot containing quadrilateral ABCD: D top left, A top right, C bottom left, B bottom right. Diagonals AC and BD cross at the centre. Equal marks (double tick) on the segments from the centre toward C and toward B, indicating AC = BD.

A.why: Equal diagonals/chords exercise figure.

B.why: Equal diagonals/chords in a circle relate chords and arcs.

entries.text: Circle with centre M (dashed radii MD and MB), points A at top, B at right, C at bottom, D at left on the circle. Quadrilateral ABCD drawn with diagonal AC through M (diameter). Sides CD and CB marked with equal tick marks (double ticks). Dashed segments MD and MB.

A.why: Equal chords and arcs exercise figure.

B.why: Equal chords CD and CB in a circle illustrate the equal arcs/chords corollary.

lessons.title: The relation between the inscribed and central angles subtended by the same arc

objectives.label: Inscribed and central angle relation
objectives.description: Calculate the measure of an inscribed angle or of the central angle subtended by the same arc, using the theorem that the inscribed angle is half the central angle.

objectives.label: Inscribed angle and arc measure
objectives.description: Calculate an inscribed angle from its subtended arc, find arc measures from angles, and show that an angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

objectives.label: Angles from intersecting chords and rays
objectives.description: Calculate the angle formed by two chords intersecting inside a circle, or by two rays intersecting outside it, using half the sum or half the difference of the intercepted arcs.

entries.text: Circle with centre M passing through vertices A (top), B (bottom right), C (bottom left) of an equilateral triangle ABC, with equal-side tick marks on the three sides; segments MB and MC drawn from the centre M. Regions between triangle and circle shaded orange.

A.why: Figure of the activity relating inscribed and central angles in the equilateral triangle.

B.why: Opening activity with equilateral triangle in circle, filed with the central angle activity.

entries.text: Inscribed angle: an angle whose vertex lies on the circle and whose sides contain two chords of the circle.

A.why: Defines the inscribed angle used in the central-angle relation.

B.why: Defines the inscribed angle used in the theorem.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; points C (top), A (right), B (lower left) on the circle. Solid chords CB and CA form inscribed angle ACB; dashed radii MB and MA form the central angle AMB.

A.why: Shows inscribed angle ACB and central angle AMB on the same arc.

B.why: Shows inscribed angle ACB and central angle AMB subtended by the same arc.

entries.text: $\angle ACB$ is an inscribed angle and $\widehat{AB}$ is the arc opposite to it.

A.why: Names the inscribed angle and its opposite arc, setting up the theorem.

B.why: Names the inscribed angle and its opposite arc, setting up the theorem.

entries.text: For each inscribed angle, there is one central angle subtended by the same arc.

A.why: Each inscribed angle has a central angle on the same arc.

B.why: Each inscribed angle has one central angle on the same arc.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, radii MA and MB drawn forming central angle AMB; A at lower right, B at lower left. Blue shading.

A.why: Illustrates the central angle AMB.

B.why: Central angle AMB is introduced alongside the inscribed angle relation.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and diameter AD (A at top, D at bottom). Points C (left) and B (right) on the circle. Chords AC and AB drawn, radii MC and MB drawn. Angles at A marked 30° (between AC and AD) and 40° (between AD and AB).

A.why: Diameter AD activity comparing inscribed and central angles.

B.why: Angles at A of 30° and 40° with radii relate to central angles.

entries.text: Case 1: circle with centre M on side CA... M lies on chord CB; points C (top), A (right), B (bottom); segments CA, MA, with C, M, B collinear.

A.why: Case 1 of the theorem's proof.

B.why: Case 1 of the proof of the inscribed-central theorem.

entries.text: Case 2: circle with M inside angle ACB; points C (top), B (left), A (right-bottom), M inside; dashed line through C, M to bottom; segments CB, CA, MB, MA.

A.why: Case 2 of the theorem's proof.

B.why: Case 2 of the proof of the inscribed-central theorem.

entries.text: Case 3: circle with M outside the inscribed angle; points C (top right), A (right), B (bottom), M (left of angle); dashed line through C, M extended; segments MA, MB, CA, CB.

A.why: Case 3 of the theorem's proof.

B.why: Case 3 of the proof of the inscribed-central theorem.

entries.text: Drill 1: circle with centre M; inscribed angle at C labelled x° subtended by arc AB; central angle BMA = 110°. Points C, B, A. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill: find inscribed angle from central angle 110°.

B.why: Central angle 110° gives inscribed angle x in a drill.

entries.text: Drill 2: circle centre M; inscribed angle ACB = 40°; central angle AMB = (y + 10)° marked with arrow. Points C, B, A. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill: find central angle from inscribed angle.

B.why: Inscribed angle 40° gives central angle in a drill.

entries.text: Drill 3: circle centre M; inscribed angle at C = 70°; central angle AMB (arrow) = (3Z + 20)°. Points C, B, A. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill: central angle from inscribed 70°.

B.why: Inscribed angle 70° gives central angle in a drill.

entries.text: Drill 4: circle centre M; inscribed angle ACB = 115°; central angle AMB = (3L + 10)°. Points C, B, A. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill: central angle from inscribed 115°.

B.why: Inscribed angle 115° gives central angle in a drill.

entries.text: Drill 5: circle centre M; angle at C = 45°; triangle MAB/ABC with angle at A marked x°. Points C, B, A. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill using inscribed-central relation.

B.why: Drill with centre M and inscribed angle 45°.

entries.text: Drill 6: circle centre M; angle at B = 25°, angle at A = 32°, angle at M marked y°. Points C, B, A. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill using inscribed-central relation.

B.why: Drill with centre M finding central angle from inscribed angles.

entries.text: Drill 7: circle centre M; chords/diameter AD through M; angle marked (Z - 15)° (arrow) at C; angle 85° at M. Points C, D, B, A. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill relating angle at C to central angle 85°.

B.why: Drill with centre M, central angle 85° and inscribed angle.

entries.text: Drill 8: circle centre M; angle at C = L°; angle at A = 55°; marked parallel sides (arrows) CA and BM. Points C, A, B, M. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill with inscribed and central angles.

B.why: Drill with centre M and inscribed angles.

entries.text: Drill 9: circle centre M; central angle AMB = (x + 135)°; inscribed angle at C = x°. Points B, A, C. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill: central angle x+135 and inscribed x.

B.why: Central angle (x+135) and inscribed angle x drill.

entries.text: Drill 10: circle centre M; angle at C = y°; angle at B = 50°; angle at A marked Z° (arrow); tick marks on sides CB and MA/BA. Points C, B, A, M. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill with inscribed and central angles.

B.why: Drill with centre M using inscribed and central angles.

entries.text: Drill 11: circle centre M with rectangle ABCD inscribed, diagonals through M; angle at C = x°, angle at D = y°, angle at A = 40°. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill with inscribed and central angles in rectangle.

B.why: Drill with rectangle diagonals through M using inscribed and central angles.

entries.text: Drill 12: circle centre M; BA is a diameter through M; C on circle; angle at C = y°, angle at B = x°, angle at A = 40°. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill with inscribed and central angles on a diameter.

B.why: Drill with centre M and diameter finding angles via inscribed-central relation.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; tangent from A touching the circle at B (arrow beyond B); line through D, M, C, A on a horizontal line with D on the left, C on the circle and A outside to the right; chord DB drawn; dashed radius MB; angle at A marked 40°.

A.why: Exercise using central and inscribed angle on arc BC.

B.why: Tangent figure with centre M uses central and inscribed angle relation.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; triangle DBA inscribed with D at top, B bottom left, A bottom right; chord AB with C its midpoint marked, MC perpendicular to AB (right angle mark at C); MA drawn; dashed MB.

A.why: Exercise using central and inscribed angle relation.

B.why: Inscribed triangle with centre M and chord AB relates inscribed and central angles.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, points A, B, C on the circle; inscribed angle ACB and central angle AMB subtended by arc AB; chords CB, CA, MB, MA drawn.

A.why: Figure for Corollary 1, inscribed angle as half the arc.

B.why: Shows inscribed angle ACB and central angle AMB on the same arc AB.

entries.text: Corollary (2): The inscribed angle drawn in a semicircle is a right angle.

A.why: Corollary 2: angle in a semicircle is right.

B.why: Corollary (2): angle in a semicircle is a right angle.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; AB is a diameter through M; point C on the circle; triangle ABC drawn with inscribed angle C subtended by the semicircle AB.

A.why: Illustrates the angle in a semicircle.

B.why: Angle C in a semicircle on diameter AB is a right angle.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, inscribed triangle ABC; arc AB labelled 4x°, arc BC labelled 5x°, arc AC labelled 3x°.

A.why: Finding angles from arc measures 4x, 5x, 3x.

B.why: Arcs in ratio 4x, 5x, 3x give inscribed angles from arc measures.

entries.text: Drill figure 1: circle, points A, B, C; arc marked 110°, arc 92° near C–A, angle at B (x + 1)°; blanks x = ..., m(AB) = ...

A.why: Drill relating arcs and inscribed angle.

B.why: Drill finding arc measures from an inscribed angle and arcs.

entries.text: Drill figure 2: circle with triangle ABC, arc 140° near B–C, angle 60° at C-side; blanks m(∠A), m(arc AC).

A.why: Drill relating arcs and inscribed angle.

B.why: Drill finding an angle and arc from given arc and angle.

entries.text: Drill figure 3: circle with diameter BA through centre M, point C, arc 128° between B and C; blanks m(∠C), m(∠B).

A.why: Drill with diameter and arc measure.

B.why: Drill using a diameter and arc 128° to find inscribed angles.

entries.text: Drill figure 4: circle with triangle ABC, equal-arc tick marks on arcs; blank m(∠C).

A.why: Drill with equal arcs giving inscribed angle.

B.why: Drill finding an angle from equal arcs of the inscribed triangle.

entries.text: Drill figure 5: circle with E, D, C, B; lines from E through D and from C through B extended to A outside; arc 104°; tick marks; blank m(∠EAC).

A.why: Angle formed by rays meeting outside the circle.

B.why: Drill with rays meeting at A outside the circle using arcs.

entries.text: Drill figure 6: circle with quadrilateral DABC and diagonal DB, angle 30° at D, arc 90° near D–A; blank m(∠DCB).

A.why: Drill finding inscribed angle from arcs.

B.why: Drill finding an angle from given arc measures.

entries.text: Circle with chords AB and CD... chords through D–E–... and B–E–A... intersecting at E; dashed segment AD; angle at E marked; points D, A, E, C, B.

A.why: Chords intersecting inside the circle at E.

B.why: Chords intersecting at E inside the circle illustrate the chord-intersection angle.

entries.text: Circle with points A, B, C, D on it. Chord line from A through B extends to E outside the circle; line from C through D extends to E. Dashed segment BC drawn. Angle at E marked. Centre marked with a dot.

A.why: Rays meeting outside the circle at E.

B.why: Two lines meeting at E outside the circle illustrate the angle from two rays outside.

entries.text: Circle with points E (top), D (right), B and C on the lower part, A outside to the right. Rays from A through D to E and through B to C; chords CD and BE intersect at X (marked x). Angle at C (BCD) marked 26°, angle at A marked 40°.

A.why: Chords inside and rays outside, angles from intercepted arcs.

B.why: Chords meeting at X and rays meeting at A belong to the intersecting chords and rays worked example.

entries.text: Circle with points E, D, B, C on it and A outside right. Rays A through D to E and A through B to C. Arc EC marked 104° on the left side, angle A marked 36°. Tick marks on arc DE (near E) and arc BC (near C) show they are equal.

A.why: Rays meeting outside at A, arcs intercepted.

B.why: Rays from A outside with arcs 104° and equal arcs illustrate the angle between two outside rays.

lessons.title: Inscribed Angles Subtended by the Same Arc

objectives.label: Inscribed angles on the same arc
objectives.description: Find the measures of inscribed angles subtended by the same arc, and use their equality to solve for unknown angles and prove relations (e.g. equal segments).

objectives.label: Equal arcs, equal angles
objectives.description: Use equal arcs (and equal chords) in the same or congruent circles to show inscribed angles are equal, and the converse, to calculate unknowns and prove triangles isosceles.

objectives.label: Show points are concyclic
objectives.description: Decide whether four points lie on one circle by checking that two equal angles are drawn on the same base and on the same side of it.

entries.text: Circle with points A, B, C, D, E on it forming a pentagon ABCDE (in order A, B, C, D, E around the circle) with diagonals drawn from D to A and B, and from E to B and C... chords AD, AE, AC, BD, BE drawn; centre marked with a dot; arc AB labelled 100° below the figure.

A.why: Arc AB = 100° figure introduces inscribed angles on the same arc.

B.why: Arc AB = 100° with inscribed angles on it, from the opening activity.

entries.text: Circle with centre dot and points A, B, C, D, E; chords AB, BC, CA, BD, DA, BE, EA drawn, showing inscribed angles C, D, E subtending arc AB.

A.why: Shows inscribed angles C, D, E subtending arc AB.

B.why: Inscribed angles C, D, E all subtend arc AB.

entries.text: Drill figure 1: circle with points A, B, C, D on it; angle 50° marked at A (between chords at A), angle 25° marked at D/C side. Values read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill finding angles from inscribed angles on the same arc.

B.why: Drill figure: equal inscribed angles on the same arc.

entries.text: Drill figure 2: circle with points A, B, C, D; angle 20° marked at A, angle 70° marked at D; tick marks on two chords. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill on equal inscribed angles standing on the same arc.

B.why: Drill figure using inscribed angles on the same arc.

entries.text: Drill figure 3: circle with points D, E, B, C on it and point A outside; angle 43° at A, angle 20° at C. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill finding unknown angle using equality of angles on the same arc.

B.why: Drill figure finding an unknown angle from inscribed angles on the same arc.

entries.text: Example 1 figure: circle with points D, A (top), B, C (bottom); chords AB and CD intersect at E; chord DA and BC drawn; tick marks on EA and ED.

A.why: Example proving equal segments using angles on the same arc.

B.why: Example 1 figure: use equal inscribed angles on the same arc to prove EA = ED.

entries.text: Two intersecting circles M and N meeting at A and B. Points F, A, C, D, E, B on the circles; line through D, A, C and line through F, A, E; chords drawn to B (BF, BD, BC, BE). Centres N and M marked. Positions read from figure; verify.

A.why: Two circles with equal arcs giving equal inscribed angles.

B.why: Two circles figure that leads into equal arcs and equal angles.

entries.text: In the circle M, if $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{DF})$ then $m(\angle B) = m(\angle E)$. $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{DF}) \Rightarrow m(\angle B) = m(\angle E)$

A.why: Equal arcs in the same circle give equal inscribed angles.

B.why: In one circle, equal arcs give equal inscribed angles.

entries.text: Circle M with points E, B on top, F, A on the sides, D, C at bottom; inscribed angles B (subtending arc AC) and E (subtending arc DF). Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Illustrates equal arcs AC and DF with equal angles B and E in circle M.

B.why: Equal arcs AC and DF in one circle with inscribed angles B and E.

entries.text: For any two circles M and N, if $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{DF})$ then $m(\angle B) = m(\angle E)$. $m(\widehat{AC}) = m(\widehat{DF}) \Rightarrow m(\angle B) = m(\angle E)$

A.why: Equal arcs in two circles give equal inscribed angles.

B.why: Equal arcs in two circles give equal inscribed angles.

entries.text: Two circles: N (green) with points E, F, D and inscribed angle E; M (pink) with points B, C, A and inscribed angle B. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Illustrates equal angles on equal arcs in two circles.

B.why: Two circles with equal arcs and their inscribed angles.

entries.text: Converse of the previous corollary (point 3): in the same circle or in congruent circles, inscribed angles of equal measures subtend arcs of equal measures.

A.why: Converse: equal inscribed angles subtend equal arcs.

B.why: Converse: equal inscribed angles subtend equal arcs.

entries.text: Drill figure 1: circle with points E, B, F, D, C, A. Angle $30^\circ$ marked at F (between FE and FD). Angle $(5x-40)^\circ$ marked at B (between BE-side and BC-side chords). Tick marks on arcs FD and CA (equal arcs). Answer line 'X = ............'.

A.why: Drill using equal arcs to get equal angles.

B.why: Equal arcs FD and CA marked, so inscribed angles are equal.

entries.text: Drill figure 2: circle with points E, B, A, D, C. Chords BA and DC are parallel (arrow marks). Angle $(3y-5)^\circ$ at E (between EB and ED); angle $50^\circ$ marked near A/C. Answer line 'Y = ............'.

A.why: Drill with parallel chords giving equal arcs and angles.

B.why: Parallel chords give equal arcs, so equal inscribed angles.

entries.text: Drill figure 3: two concentric circles with centre M and points E, B, C, F, D, A. Angle $56^\circ$ at E in the inner circle; angle $(2z+6)^\circ$ at B in the outer circle. Answer line 'Z = ............'.

A.why: Drill with equal arcs in concentric circles and equal angles.

B.why: Exercise figure using equal arcs and equal angles across circles.

objectives.label: Identify cyclic quadrilaterals
objectives.description: Determine whether a given quadrilateral is a cyclic quadrilateral by checking whether two angles drawn on the same base and in one direction of it are equal, and explain the answer.

objectives.label: Prove a figure is cyclic
objectives.description: Prove that a figure is a cyclic quadrilateral by showing two equal angles (such as two right angles, or angles from parallel lines) on the same base and in one direction of it.

objectives.label: Use cyclic property in deductions
objectives.description: Use a proven cyclic quadrilateral and its circle to deduce equal angles, parallel lines and the location of the centre of the circle through its vertices.

entries.text: Quadrilateral ABCD with vertices D top-left, A top-right, B bottom-right, C bottom-left; diagonals AC and BD intersect at E. Angle at A (CAD) marked 35°, angle at E (CED) marked 93°, angle at C (ACB) marked 58°.

A.why: Activity figure with equal angles on a base, deciding if ABCD is cyclic.

B.why: Activity figure with angles 35°, 58° on base AD to decide whether ABCD is cyclic.

entries.text: A cyclic quadrilateral is a quadrilateral figure whose four vertices belong to one circle.

A.why: Defines a cyclic quadrilateral, introducing the lesson as a whole.

B.why: Defines a cyclic quadrilateral, the basis for identifying one.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; quadrilateral ABCD inscribed with vertices A (top), B (right), C (bottom), D (left) on the circle.

A.why: Illustrates the definition with vertices on one circle, not a specific skill.

B.why: Shows an inscribed quadrilateral ABCD on circle M as an example of a cyclic quadrilateral.

entries.text: The figure ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral because its vertices A, B, C and D belong to the circle M.

A.why: Restates the definition applied to the circle figure, introductory.

B.why: Explains why ABCD is cyclic: its vertices lie on circle M, the meaning of cyclic.

entries.text: Quadrilateral XYZL with L top-left, X right, Y bottom-right, Z bottom-left; diagonals XZ and YL drawn; angle at L (YLZ) and angle at X (YXZ) marked equal.

A.why: Shows equal angles on a base in one direction, the test for a cyclic quadrilateral.

B.why: Illustrates equal angles YLZ and YXZ on base YZ showing XYZL is cyclic.

entries.text: The figure XYZL is a cyclic quadrilateral because m(∠YXZ) = m(∠YLZ): they are two drawn angles on the base YZ and in one direction of it, so a circle can be drawn passing through the points X, Y, Z and L, i.e. the vertices of figure XYZL belong to one circle. $m(\angle YXZ)=m(\angle YLZ)$

A.why: States the rule: equal angles on the same base in one direction mean the figure is cyclic.

B.why: States the test: equal angles on the same base and in one direction mean the quadrilateral is cyclic.

entries.text: Drill figure 1: quadrilateral ADBC (rhombus-like kite) with diagonals AC and DB meeting at E with a right-angle mark; angle at D = 40°, angle at B = 50° (angles ADB and DBA read from figure; verify). Vertices A top, D left, B right, C bottom.

A.why: Drill figure asking which figure is cyclic and why.

B.why: Drill figure 1 asks which figure is cyclic.

entries.text: Drill figure 2: triangle DCB with point A on DB side; CA drawn; right-angle mark at A; angle at C = 40°, angle at B = 50°. Points D, A, B, C (read from figure; verify).

A.why: Drill figure asking which figure is cyclic and why.

B.why: Drill figure 2 asks which figure is cyclic, with right angles/angle checks.

entries.text: Drill figure 3: trapezium DABC with DA parallel to CB (arrow marks); diagonals DB and AC intersect; angle at D = 41° (angle between DA and diagonal), angle between diagonals = 99°.

A.why: Drill figure asking which figure is cyclic and why.

B.why: Drill figure 3 asks which figure is cyclic, with angles on the same base DA.

entries.text: Drill figure 4: quadrilateral DABC, parallelogram-like with tick marks showing opposite sides equal (DA and CB, DC and AB).

A.why: Drill figure asking which figure is cyclic and why.

B.why: Drill figure 4 asks which figure is cyclic.

entries.text: Drill figure 5: trapezium DABC with DA parallel to CB (arrow marks) and non-parallel sides DC and AB marked with tick marks as equal.

A.why: Drill figure asking which figure is cyclic and why.

B.why: Drill figure 5 asks which figure is cyclic, checking equal angles on a base.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; AB horizontal diameter (B left, A right); chord AC with C at top left, X midpoint of AC marked with ticks; line from X through M to Y below B; BY tangent at B going down to Y; AY joined.

A.why: Worked example figure proving a figure is cyclic with AB diameter and midpoint X.

B.why: Figure for the worked example with diameter AB and midpoint X, proving a figure is cyclic.

entries.text: Circle with center M and points C, A, B on it. Chords AB and AC are drawn from A, with C at left, A at right, B at bottom. Points x (on AB) and y (on AC) are marked as midpoints with tick marks. M is joined to A, C, B, x and y. Labels read from figure; verify.

A.why: Exercise figure with midpoints x and y, proving a figure is cyclic.

B.why: Figure for the exercise with midpoints X and Y of chords in circle M, proving a figure cyclic.

entries.text: Circle with cyclic quadrilateral ABCD (D top-left, A top-right, B bottom-right, C bottom-left). Diagonals AC and BD meet at F. X lies on AF, Y lies on DF, with XY drawn parallel to AD (arrow marks on AD and XY). B and C are joined to X and Y. Points read from figure; verify.

A.why: Worked example figure proving a quadrilateral is cyclic using parallel lines.

B.why: Figure for the worked example proving a figure cyclic using XY parallel to AD.

entries.text: Circle with cyclic quadrilateral ABCD (D top-left, A top-right, B bottom-right, C bottom-left). Diagonals AC and BD are drawn; AE and DF are drawn as angle bisectors, with E and F marked near the bottom between the diagonals, joined by EF. Angle marks at A and D; arrows at B and C region. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Exercise figure with angle bisectors, proving a figure is cyclic.

B.why: Cyclic quadrilateral with angle bisectors AE and DF is a proof-that-figure-is-cyclic setup, like the exercise with bisector AE.

objectives.label: Opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral
objectives.description: Calculate unknown angles (and arcs) in a cyclic quadrilateral using the fact that each two opposite angles are supplementary.

objectives.label: Exterior angle of cyclic quadrilateral
objectives.description: Calculate angle measures using the corollary that the exterior angle at a vertex of a cyclic quadrilateral equals the interior angle at the opposite vertex.

objectives.label: Prove a quadrilateral is cyclic
objectives.description: Prove that a quadrilateral is cyclic using the converse (supplementary opposite angles) or an exterior angle equal to the interior opposite angle.

entries.text: Circle with centre dot and inscribed quadrilateral ABCD (vertices A top, B right, C bottom right, D left); angle at A marked 60°. Used in the Think and Discuss.

A.why: Figure for the Think and Discuss on the sum of opposite angles.

B.why: Figure for the Think and Discuss on the sum of opposite angles.

entries.text: Circle with centre dot and inscribed quadrilateral ABCD (A top, B right, C bottom right, D left), used for the proof of Theorem 3.

A.why: Figure used in the proof of Theorem 3 on opposite angles.

B.why: Figure for the proof of Theorem 3 on opposite angles.

entries.text: Drill figure 1: circle with quadrilateral ABCD; angle A = 4y°, D = 107°, C = 5x°, B = (2x+7)°. Centre marked by a dot. Points read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill figure finding unknown opposite angles in a cyclic quadrilateral.

B.why: Exercise figure finding x and y from supplementary opposite angles.

entries.text: Drill figure 2: circle with quadrilateral ABCD; angle D = 115°, A = 2x°, C = 2y°, B = (x+15)°. Verify from figure.

B.why: Exercise figure finding x and y from supplementary opposite angles.

entries.text: Drill figure 3: circle with centre M, diameter CB... line from C through M to B; points D and A on circle; angle C = 70°, angle A = 2x°, angle B = y°; tick marks on DA and AB. Verify from figure.

A.why: Drill figure with unknown angles in a cyclic quadrilateral.

B.why: Exercise figure finding x and y from supplementary opposite angles.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, AB a vertical diameter, D and C on the circle, dashed BD drawn, angle C = 140°, tick marks on CB and CD. Verify from figure.

A.why: Drill figure with angle C = 140° in a cyclic quadrilateral.

B.why: Exercise figure finding angles with opposite angles supplementary.

entries.text: Drill A figure: circle with quadrilateral ABCD and diagonal BD; 30° at D, 70° at C. Verify.

A.why: Drill A figure in the opposite-angle exercise.

B.why: Exercise figure finding angles in a cyclic quadrilateral.

entries.text: Drill B figure: circle with centre M, triangle/quadrilateral ABCD, angles 2x° marked at M (two). Verify.

A.why: Drill B figure in the opposite-angle exercise.

B.why: Exercise figure finding the value of x using opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral.

entries.text: Drill C figure: circle with centre M on BA, points C, D above; 60° near C/D, 80° at A. Verify.

A.why: Drill C figure in the opposite-angle exercise.

B.why: Exercise figure finding unknown angles in a circle with quadrilateral.

entries.text: Drill D figure: circle with ABCD, E; 95° at A, 28° at D, arrows marking parallel sides. Verify.

A.why: Drill D figure in the opposite-angle exercise.

B.why: Exercise figure finding unknown angles in a cyclic quadrilateral.

entries.text: Circle with centre marked, cyclic quadrilateral ABCD (A bottom left, B bottom right, C top right, D top left), side AB extended beyond B to point E with arrow; right-angle-like arc mark at D and arc mark at exterior angle EBC.

A.why: Figure showing the exterior angle at B of a cyclic quadrilateral.

B.why: Figure showing the exterior angle EBC of a cyclic quadrilateral for the corollary.

entries.text: Circle with cyclic quadrilateral ABCD and diagonal DB; AB extended beyond B to E; exterior angle CBE marked 85°; arc AB marked 110°. Points read from figure; verify.

A.why: Figure for the worked example on the exterior angle CBE.

B.why: Worked example figure with exterior angle CBE = 85° and arc AB = 110°.

entries.text: Quadrilateral ABCD drawn with a dashed circle through its vertices; A at top right, D upper left, C bottom left, B bottom right; centre marked by a dot.

A.why: Figure of a quadrilateral with a dashed circle for the converse proof.

B.why: Quadrilateral with a dashed circle through its vertices illustrates the converse making it cyclic.

entries.text: Drill 1 figure: quadrilateral ABCD with D top left, A top right, B bottom right, C bottom left; angle at A is 97°, angle at C is 83°.

A.why: Drill figure proving ABCD cyclic from supplementary opposite angles 97° and 83°.

A.why: Drill figure for proving ABCD is cyclic.

B.why: Drill 2 figure with given angles used to prove ABCD is cyclic.

entries.text: Drill 3 figure: kite-like quadrilateral with D at top, A at right, B at bottom, C at left; diagonal from C to A; 40° marked at the left near the diagonal's end, 80° at B; tick marks on equal sides.

A.why: Drill figure for proving ABCD is cyclic.

B.why: Drill 3 figure with angles 40° and 80° to prove the figure is cyclic.

entries.text: Corollary: If the measure of the exterior angle at a vertex of a quadrilateral figure is equal to the measure of the interior angle at the opposite vertex, then the figure is a cyclic quadrilateral.

A.why: Corollary giving the exterior-angle test for a cyclic quadrilateral.

B.why: Corollary stating a quadrilateral is cyclic when its exterior angle equals the opposite interior angle.

entries.text: Quadrilateral ABCD with A bottom left, B bottom right, C top right, D top left; side AB extended to the right through B to point E with an arrow.

A.why: Figure with AB extended to E illustrating the exterior-angle test.

B.why: Figure for the corollary of the converse: exterior angle at B equal to interior opposite angle.

entries.text: Second drill 1 figure: quadrilateral ABCD with D upper left, A top right, B bottom right, C bottom left; exterior angle 86° at A (with E on the extension), exterior angle 94° at C (with F on extension of BC).

entries.text: Second drill 2 figure: quadrilateral ABCD with D at top, A right, B bottom, C bottom left; diagonal DB; E on extension of CB to the left; 120° exterior angle at C; 30° at B; tick marks on sides.

A.why: Drill figure with exterior angle at C to prove cyclic.

B.why: Second drill on proving ABCD cyclic using the 120° exterior angle and interior angle.

entries.text: Second drill 3 figure: trapezium ABCD with DA parallel to CB (parallel arrows); D top left, A top right, B bottom right, C bottom; angle 74° at B; F above C with 53° marked with equal-angle marks at C; E to the left on line BC extended.

A.why: Drill figure with exterior angle to prove cyclic.

B.why: Second drill figure with exterior angle at C to find angles using the exterior-angle corollary.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and horizontal diameter AB (B at left, A at right). Chords AC and AD from A with C and D on the upper part of the circle. The small region XYDC is shaded yellow; a short dashed mark is on segment BC (drawn line BC). Labels: Y, D, X, C, B, M, A.

B.why: Circle with tangent and chords is a general challenge figure not tied to one objective.

Perpendiculars from vertices: AE to BC (E on BC, right-angle mark at E), BF to line AC extended (arrow beyond F), CD to AB (right-angle mark at D). They intersect at point x inside the triangle. A dashed segment from D to E. Labels: A, F, D, x, C, E, B.

B.why: Orthocentre-type triangle figure with perpendiculars is not about cyclic quadrilateral angle properties taught here; unspecific.

lessons.title: The relation between the tangents of a circle

objectives.label: Tangent segments from a point outside a circle
objectives.description: Use the equality of the two tangent segments drawn to a circle from a point outside it, and the corollaries (the line through the centre and the intersection point of the tangents is the axis of the chord of tangency and bisects the angle between the tangents), to find unknown lengths and angle measures and to prove relations.

objectives.label: Circle inscribed in a polygon
objectives.description: Use the circle inscribed in a polygon (touching all of its sides internally) and equal tangent segments to find the perimeter and area of the polygon and the position of the centre.

objectives.label: Common tangents of two circles
objectives.description: Distinguish common internal and common external tangents of two circles, and solve problems finding unknown values and the length of a common tangent.

entries.text: Circle with centre M and horizontal diameter AB; right-angle marks at A and B; tangents L1 at A and L2 at B drawn vertically upward with arrows, parallel.

A.why: Tangent perpendicular to the diameter is lesson-introduction background, not a specific objective.

B.why: Parallel tangents at ends of a diameter, introductory prior knowledge.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; chord AB labelled 'tangent chord'; tangent L2 at A and tangent L1 at B meet at point C outside the circle; segments CA and CB labelled 'tangent segment'.

A.why: Shows the two tangents at the ends of a chord meeting at C with tangent segments CA and CB.

B.why: Tangents at ends of a chord meeting at C; tangent segments.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; external point A to the right; tangent segments AC (upper) and AB (lower) touching the circle at C and B; dashed lines MA, MC, MB.

A.why: Illustrates the two tangent segments from an external point A, as in Theorem 4.

B.why: Tangent segments AC and AB from external point A for Theorem 4.

entries.text: Circle M with tangent segments AB and AC from external point A, chord BC meeting line MA at D, radii MB and MC; line MA drawn with arrows; points C, M, D, A, B labelled.

A.why: Shows line MA and chord BC, used for the corollary about the axis of the chord.

B.why: Tangent segments from A with line MA meeting chord BC.

entries.text: The straight line passing through the center of the circle and the intersection point of the two tangents is an axis of symmetry to the chord of tangency of those two tangents.

A.why: Corollary: line through the centre and the tangents' intersection is the axis of the chord of tangency.

B.why: Corollary: line through centre and tangents' intersection is axis of the chord of tangency.

entries.text: Circle M with tangents AB and AC from A touching at B and C; line MA through M and A; chord BC meets MA at D with a right-angle mark; equal tick marks on BD and CD.

A.why: Shows MA perpendicular to and bisecting chord BC, illustrating the corollary.

B.why: MA is the axis of chord BC of tangency.

entries.text: Circle M with tangents AB and AC from A touching at B and C; line MA through M and A; radii MB and MC with equal angle marks at M and equal angle marks at A.

A.why: Shows MA bisecting the angle between the tangents, illustrating the corollary.

B.why: MA bisects the angle between the tangents (corollary).

entries.text: Drill figure 1: circle M with tangent points C (top) and B (bottom), external point A. Radii MC and MB drawn, chord CB. Angle at A = 50°; angle at M between MC and chord CB marked y°, angle at M between chord CB and MB marked z° (z next to M); angle x° at B between chord BC and BA.

A.why: Drill finding angle measures from tangents from a point outside.

B.why: Tangent segments from A used to find angles x, y, z.

entries.text: Drill figure 2: circle M with tangent points C (top) and B (bottom), external point A to the right; segment MA drawn. Angle at M between MC and MA is y°, angle between MA and MB is z°; angle at A between AC and AM is 35°, angle between AM and AB is x°.

A.why: Drill finding angles using MA bisecting the angle between tangents.

B.why: Line MA bisects the angle between tangents; find angles.

entries.text: Drill figure 3: circle M with point D on circle at upper left, tangent points C (top) and B (bottom), external point A. Angle z° at D, angle y° at C, angle x° at A. Tangent segments AC and AB marked equal with tick marks; MC, MB, DC, DB drawn.

A.why: Drill finding angles with equal tangent segments AC and AB.

B.why: Equal tangent segments AC and AB used to find angles.

entries.text: Circle with points A (bottom), B (left), C (top), D (top right) on it. Tangent rays at A (to the right) and at B (upward) meeting at X (bottom left); angle at X = 70°; angle at C (DCB) = 125°. Chords BA, BC, CD, DA drawn.

A.why: Exercise finding angles with two tangents meeting at X.

B.why: Tangents meeting at X used to find angle measures.

entries.text: Circle M with points C, D, B on it; tangent segments AB and AC drawn from external point A; chord CD and radii/segments MB, MD, MC drawn; BC drawn; angle at M between MD and MB marked 130°. Arrows marked on CD and AB showing parallel.

A.why: Exercise using tangent segments AB and AC to find angles and prove parallelism.

B.why: Tangents AB and AC from A used to find angle measures.

entries.text: Circle M with points C, D, B; external point A with tangents AB and AC; X on BC and on AM; M center; Y on chord BD with tick marks showing Y midpoint of BD; segment XY and MY drawn; angle at Y between YX and YM marked 35°; lower-case 'y' labelled.

A.why: Exercise using tangents from A and the line AM through the centre to find an angle.

B.why: Tangents from A with line AM and chord BC used to find an angle.

entries.text: Triangle ABC with circle M inside touching sides at D (on AB... side AB right), E (on CB), F (on AC). Vertices A top, C bottom left, B bottom right. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Circle inscribed in triangle ABC touching its sides.

B.why: Circle inscribed in triangle ABC touching its sides.

entries.text: Quadrilateral ABCD with inscribed circle M (blue) touching AD at L, AB at X, CB at Y, CD at Z. Radius R drawn from M to Y. Dashed lines from M to vertices. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Circle inscribed in quadrilateral ABCD touching its sides.

B.why: Circle M inscribed in quadrilateral ABCD touching all sides.

entries.text: Drill 1: circle with centre M, radius 5 cm (MB = 5 cm). Tangent segments AC and AB from external point A; points C, B on circle; D on segment MA where it meets the circle. Labels: 12 cm along CA, y cm along DA, x cm along AB. Read from figure; verify.

B.why: Two circles with common tangents meeting at A, finding unknown values.

entries.text: Drill 3: triangle ABC with a circle inscribed touching AC at F, AB at D, and BC at F (second touch point); AF = 5 cm (side AC upper part), AB part 6 cm, lower AC part y cm, BC part x cm, BC = 7 cm. Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Drill using a circle inscribed in a triangle to find side lengths.

B.why: Circle inscribed in triangle ABC with equal tangent segments to find lengths.

entries.text: (A) The line AB is called a common internal tangent to the two circles M and N because the two circles are located at two different sides of AB; also CD is an internal tangent to the two circles.

A.why: Defines the common internal tangent of two circles.

B.why: Defines the common internal tangent of two circles.

entries.text: Notice that the segments AB and CD intersect at E. $\overline{AB}\cap\overline{CD}=\{E\}$

A.why: Notes that the internal tangent segments intersect, distinguishing internal tangents.

B.why: Notes that the internal tangent segments meet at E.

entries.text: Two separate circles, N (left, small) and M (right, large). Internal tangent lines AB and CD cross at F between the circles. A, B on line AB (A touching M, B touching N); D, C on line CD (D touching N, C touching M). Read from figure; verify.

B.why: Common internal tangents AB and CD of two circles.

A.why: Notes that the external tangent rays intersect, distinguishing external tangents.

B.why: Notes that the external tangent rays meet at F.

entries.text: Small circle N and large circle M on the same side of two external tangent lines AB and CD, which meet at F on the left. B on N, A on M (line AB); D on N, C on M (line CD). Read from figure; verify.

A.why: Shows the common external tangents of two circles.

B.why: Two external tangents of circles M and N meeting at F.

entries.text: Two externally placed circles: small circle with centre N touching the line at B, large circle with centre M touching the line at A. Common tangent line AB drawn with arrows at both ends. Dashed segment MN labelled 41 cm.

A.why: Finds the length of a common tangent AB given the distance MN.

B.why: Common tangent AB of two circles with MN given, used to find the common tangent's length.

objectives.label: Calculate angles of tangency
objectives.description: Calculate the measure of an angle of tangency (or an unknown arc) using the fact that it is half the measure of the arc between its sides, and equals the inscribed angle on the same arc or half the central angle.

objectives.label: Prove cyclic quadrilaterals
objectives.description: Prove that a quadrilateral is cyclic by using the equality of the angle of tangency with the inscribed angle together with parallel lines.

objectives.label: Prove a line is tangent
objectives.description: Show that a line is a tangent to a circle by applying the converse of theorem 5 (angle with the chord equals the inscribed angle in the alternate side).

entries.text: Circle with centre dot; point B on the circle at the bottom; ray BA going up to A; rays from B through C, D1, D2 (all on the circle's upper right, labelled C, D1, D2) as successive positions; tangent ray BD at B pointing right with D at the end. Labels read from figure; verify.

A.why: Moving ray BC to BD shows the angle of tangency growing with its arc, as in the activity.

B.why: Activity figure showing the tangent angle growing with its arc.

entries.text: The measure of angle ABD equals half the measure of arc ACD. $m(\angle ABD)=\frac{1}{2}m(\widehat{ACD})$

A.why: States that the angle of tangency is half its arc.

B.why: Angle of tangency is half its intercepted arc.

entries.text: Angle of tangency: the angle composed of the union of two rays, one a tangent to the circle and the other containing a chord of the circle passing through the point of tangency.

A.why: Defines the angle of tangency, a term for the whole lesson rather than one objective's calculation.

B.why: Defines the angle of tangency the lesson calculates.

entries.text: Circle with centre dot; chord from B (bottom left of circle) to A (upper right on circle); tangent ray at B pointing right to C. Points A, B, C labelled.

A.why: Illustrates the definition of the angle of tangency.

B.why: Figure of an angle of tangency with its chord and arc.

entries.text: Three drill figures. (1) Circle, chord AB, tangent ray BC at B, arc labelled 230° on the left. (2) Circle centre M, vertical diameter AB, tangent ray BC at B. (3) Circle with triangle DAB inscribed, three sides ticked equal, A and D at top, tangent line through B with C on right.

A.why: Drill figures for finding angles of tangency or arcs.

B.why: Drill figures for computing angles of tangency and arcs.

entries.text: Circle with inscribed triangle with vertices D, A, B; tangent ray at B going to C. Used with the proof.

A.why: Figure for the proof that the angle of tangency is half its arc.

B.why: Figure used with the proof that the angle of tangency equals the inscribed angle.

entries.text: Corollary: The measure of the angle of tangency is half the measure of the central angle subtended by the same arc.

A.why: Corollary: the angle of tangency is half the central angle on the same arc.

B.why: Corollary: angle of tangency is half the central angle on the same arc.

entries.text: Circle with centre M, points D and A on the circle, B at the bottom, inscribed triangle DAB, radii MA and MB drawn, tangent ray BC at B.

A.why: Shows the central angle and the tangent angle on the same arc for the corollary.

B.why: Figure for the corollary: tangent angle is half the central angle.

entries.text: Drill figure 1: circle with inscribed quadrilateral-like shape through D, A, B; tangent line through B and C; angle at D marked 70°, y° at the A side, x° the angle between chord BA and tangent BC at B.

A.why: Drill finding x and y from given angles and the tangency relation.

B.why: Drill figure for finding unknown angles x and y.

entries.text: Drill figure 2: circle with points E, A, D, B on it; tangent line through B and C; y° at E, 30° angle at A, x° angle at B with tangent BC.

A.why: Drill finding x and y using the angle of tangency and inscribed angle.

B.why: Drill figure for finding unknown angles x and y.

entries.text: Drill figure 3: circle with centre M, points A, D, B on it; tangent line through B and C; 25° marked at A, y° at D, x° at B with tangent.

A.why: Drill finding x and y using the angle of tangency and inscribed angle.

B.why: Drill figure for finding unknown angles x and y.

entries.text: The angle of tangency is supplementary to the inscribed angle drawn on the chord of the angle of tangency and on one side of it.

A.why: Supplementary relation of the angle of tangency and the inscribed angle, used to calculate angles.

B.why: Rule relating the angle of tangency to the inscribed angle, used in computing angles.

entries.text: i.e. angle ABC is supplementary to angle AEB. $\angle ABC$ is supplementary to $\angle AEB$

A.why: Restates the supplementary relation for angles ABC and AEB.

B.why: Symbolic statement of the supplementary relation used to compute angles.

entries.text: Circle with points D, A, E, B on it; tangent line through B and C; chord AB, chords BE and AE drawn forming angles ABC and AEB.

A.why: Illustrates the supplementary angles ABC and AEB.

B.why: Illustrates the angle of tangency and the inscribed angle on its chord.

entries.text: Drill figure 1: circle with points C, D, A on it, line through A and B tangent to circle at A; 100° marked at A.

A.why: Drill figure calculating angles from a tangent and given angle.

B.why: Drill figure for finding angles with a tangent.

entries.text: Drill figure 2: circle with centre M, points C, D, B; tangents from A meeting the circle at C and B; 125° marked near D.

A.why: Drill figure calculating angles from tangents and a given angle.

B.why: Drill figure for finding angles with tangents and arcs.

entries.text: Drill figure 3: circle with points C, B, A; 120° marked at top arc near C-B; 70° at B; tangent line through A and D.

A.why: Drill figure calculating angles with a tangent and given arcs and angles.

B.why: Drill figure for finding angles with a tangent.

entries.text: Example 1 figure: circle with inscribed triangle ABC, tangent line through B with D on it; angles x and y marked at B/near X and Y.

A.why: Example 1 figure for proving a quadrilateral cyclic using the tangent angle and a parallel chord.

B.why: Example 1 figure with tangent at B and XY, for proving the quadrilateral is cyclic.

entries.text: Circle with centre M; triangle ABC inscribed with C at left, B at upper right, A at bottom; ray AD drawn from A to the right (D). Angle at C (angle ACB) and angle DAB are marked equal.

A.why: Equal angles ACB and DAB illustrate the converse showing AD is tangent.

B.why: Figure of equal angles ACB and DAB, illustrating the converse that AD is tangent.

entries.text: Drill shape 1: triangle ABC with ray AD going up-left from A; angle between AD and AB marked 130°; angle B = 65°; tick marks on sides AC and CB (equal).

A.why: Drill shape for showing AD is a tangent.

B.why: Drill shape where one must show AD is a tangent.

entries.text: Drill shape 2: triangle ABC with ray AD going up-right from A; angle DAB = 75°; angle at A inside triangle (CAB) = 60°; angle C = 5x°; angle B = 3x°.

A.why: Drill shape for showing AD is a tangent.

B.why: Drill shape where one must show AD is a tangent.

entries.text: Drill shape 3: triangle ABC with ray AD from A; angle DAB = 60° (right-angle-like mark at A); AC = 3 cm; CB = 6 cm; tick mark on AD.

A.why: Drill shape for showing AD is a tangent.

B.why: Drill shape where one must show AD is a tangent.

entries.text: Circle with inscribed triangle ABC, tangent line through A with D on the right; chord XY drawn inside parallel to BC, with arrows marking parallel lines; points labelled x and y inside the circle near X and Y (read from figure; verify).

A.why: Chord XY parallel to BC with tangent at A, used to prove a cyclic quadrilateral.

B.why: Figure of the tangent-at-A example with XY parallel to BC, like the filed worked example proving AD is tangent.
